newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Orange pips forecasts, branches out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Orange pips forecasts, branches out.

text.p: Orange, Britain's youngest cellular group, beat forecasts on Thursday by slashing half year pre-tax losses 41 percent and said it was developing a host of advanced new services to win new customers and hang onto old ones.

Orange, which expects to break into a pre-tax profit in the first half of 1999, said first half pre-tax losses narrowed to 74 million pounds ($117.4 million) -- about 15 percent above most analysts' expectations.
Turnover jumped 67 percent to 427 million pounds.
Helped by the growing popularity of its network, Orange broke into the black for the first time on an EBIDTA level.
Earnings before interest, depreciation, tax and amortisation came in at 12 million pounds compared to a 70 million pound loss in the first half of 1996.

Orange, which reported a 13 percent rise to 500 pounds in annual revenues from each subscriber, is Britain's third biggest mobile telephone company. An aggressive marketing campaign has won the three-year-old digital operator more than one million customers and a 13.3 percent market share.

Finance director Graham Howe said the company was "poised to set the agenda for the wirefree future" by developing services such as Internet browsing, home shopping, on-line financial services, narrow-band TV, virtual banking and video telephony -- all via its handsets.
In order to be able to offer the services, Orange is doubling the strength of its network and plans to spend 800 million pounds in an accelerated network expansion programme over the next 18 months.

Orange will be using the headroom in its 1.2 billion pound debt facility, taken out in 1995, to help fund the investment and will be looking to renegotiate the facility at more favourable terms for further expansion plans.

The group's shares rose 6.5 pence to 218.5p by 1330 GMT as analysts welcomed its plans to roll out the network, reduce its already low level of subscriber defections -- or churn -- and develop new services.
But Orange's insistence that customers are more interested in quality coverage rather than in the price they have to pay for it was misplaced, some argued.

"They have underestimated significantly that there is price pressure in the market now and the extent that this will increase in the future," said Andrew Harrington, telecoms analyst at Salomon Brothers.

"They don't appreciate how poor the growth in the UK market is compared to other markets around Europe. The UK is the slowest growth market in Europe by far and there's only one thing that differentiates the UK from the rest of Europe -- and that is prices that are 50 percent higher on average."

But managing director Hans Snook said market estimates that mobile telephone penetration in Britain would rise from 13 percent to Scandinavian levels of 30 percent by 2006 were conservative -- despite current prices.

Orange, whose customers will be able to use their telephones in 78 countries over 100 networks by the end of the year, sees a future where it will take on fixed-line giants such as British Telecommunications Plc and Cable and Wireless Communications.

"There's no reason why virtually 100 percent of the adult population at some point in the future will communicate through a mobile device," finance director Howe said. "...There is no reason why you should rely on a wire in the wall."

Having won a licence as part of a consortium to operate mobile services in Austria, Orange is eyeing the Netherlands and said it was on the lookout for similar opportunities. ($ = 0.630 British Pounds)
